["SUBJECTIVE 
CHIEF COMPLAINT 
Follow-up of chronic problems. 
HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS 
Alexander is a 62-year-old male with a history of reflux presenting for follow-up. Since starting Protonix (pantoprazole) 40 mg daily, he reports marked improvement in reflux symptoms—now comfortable and able to eat whatever he wants. He has transitioned from high caffeine intake/energy drinks to green tea and is working on dietary/lifestyle modifications (cutting back on caffeine, spicy foods, and alcohol). He plans to increase his exercise. 

"ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: 
1. Gastroesophageal reflux disease with prior mild gastritis — well controlled 
Assessment: Dramatic symptomatic improvement on pantoprazole 40 mg daily. Prior endoscopy (last year) showed mild gastritis. No current GI symptoms. 
Plan: 
- Continue pantoprazole (Protonix) 40 mg daily. 
- Continue lifestyle modifications (limit caffeine/energy drinks; avoid spicy foods and alcohol). 

2. Systolic ejection murmur — stable 
Assessment: Soft 2/6 systolic ejection murmur, unchanged from prior; asymptomatic; vitals in clinic look good. No carotid bruits. 
Plan: 
- Continue routine monitoring; no changes today. 

3. Bilateral lower extremity edema — mild, likely dependent 
Assessment: 1+ pitting edema in both legs; lungs clear; patient asymptomatic. Likely mild fluid retention from prolonged standing. 
Plan: 
- Observation; no acute intervention discussed today. 

4. Blood pressure — well controlled 
Assessment: Office vitals “look really good”; patient doing a great job managing blood pressure; heart rate low. 
Plan: 
- Continue current management."]

SUBJECTIVE 
CHIEF COMPLAINT 
Facial rash follow-up.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS 
Jacqueline Miller presents for follow-up of a facial rash. She reports marked improvement when taking doxycycline twice daily for the first two weeks; after reducing to once daily last week based on pharmacist advice, the rash has plateaued and is not continuing to improve. She is not breastfeeding. Current regimen: sulfacetamide face wash twice daily (tolerated, not drying), metronidazole cream applied immediately after washing, and doxycycline (recently reduced to once daily). She did not start pimecrolimus (Elidel) due to concerns after reading about it and because it is cost-prohibitive with her insurance; she also checked prices for Eucrisa and found it more expensive. She is not using any moisturizer, Cetaphil cleanser, or Neutrogena wipes. She notes she feels sun-sensitive and is using sun precautions (hat). On clinician inspection today, there are a few faint erythematous papules on the bilateral medial cheeks and mild redness around/under the nostrils; not completely resolved.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: 
1. Perioral dermatitis 
Assessment: Improved with doxycycline BID but plateaued after self-reduction to once daily; mild residual papules and perinasal erythema on exam. Not breastfeeding. Prefers to avoid topical steroids on face. 
Plan: 
- Increase doxycycline back to twice daily until rash is completely cleared, then continue once daily for one additional week before stopping. Counsel on potential GI upset/heartburn and strong photosensitivity; continue strict sun protection. 
- Start tacrolimus ointment (non-steroidal calcineurin inhibitor): apply a thin layer to involved facial rash areas twice daily until resolved. Counsel that brief tingling/flushing may occur for a few seconds after application and is not an allergy. Avoid topical steroids on the face due to risk of worsening and skin thinning. 
- Continue sulfacetamide face wash; may reduce to once daily if any dryness develops (use as tolerated). 
- Continue metronidazole cream after washing. 
- Add bland moisturizer as needed (e.g., Vanicream; small amounts of petroleum jelly if very dry). 
- Medication list/coverage: Cancel pimecrolimus (Elidel) due to cost; clindamycin removed from list. Prescription for tacrolimus to Metro Market pharmacy as discussed. Refills for doxycycline and metronidazole are adequate.

2. Rosacea (facial) 
Assessment: Overlapping rosacea component with persistent mild erythema/papules; photosensitivity noted. 
Plan: 
- Continue metronidazole cream and gentle skincare; avoid anti-aging or botanical products until reassessed. 
- Reinforce sun protection (hat already in use); avoid known triggers when possible.

3. Ocular rosacea 
Assessment: History/concern for ocular involvement; preventive eyelid hygiene recommended. 
Plan: 
- Gently wash eyelids once daily with a gentle cleanser (e.g., Vanicream). 
- Use a Bruder warm compress mask as needed.

Follow-up instructions: 
- Follow up in approximately 4 weeks. 
- If rash worsens or fails to improve, call or send MyChart message sooner. 
- For a mild flare after clearance, may try tacrolimus alone for a couple of days; if insufficient, restart doxycycline per above schedule. 
- Hold off on starting any new skincare products until next visit; discuss any planned additions first.

SUBJECTIVE 
CHIEF COMPLAINT 
Facial rash follow-up.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS 
Jacqueline Miller presents for follow-up of a facial rash. She reports marked improvement when taking doxycycline twice daily for the first two weeks; after reducing to once daily last week based on pharmacist advice, the rash has plateaued and is not continuing to improve. She is not breastfeeding. Current regimen: sulfacetamide face wash twice daily (tolerated, not drying), metronidazole cream applied immediately after washing, and doxycycline (recently reduced to once daily). She did not start pimecrolimus (Elidel) due to concerns after reading about it and because it is cost-prohibitive with her insurance; she also checked prices for Eucrisa and found it more expensive. She is not using any moisturizer, Cetaphil cleanser, or Neutrogena wipes. She notes she feels sun-sensitive and is using sun precautions (hat). On clinician inspection today, there are a few faint erythematous papules on the bilateral medial cheeks and mild redness around/under the nostrils; not completely resolved.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: 
1. Perioral dermatitis 
Assessment: Improved with doxycycline BID but plateaued after self-reduction to once daily; mild residual papules and perinasal erythema on exam. Not breastfeeding. Prefers to avoid topical steroids on face. 
Plan: 
- Increase doxycycline back to twice daily until rash is completely cleared, then continue once daily for one additional week before stopping. Counsel on potential GI upset/heartburn and strong photosensitivity; continue strict sun protection. 
- Start tacrolimus ointment (non-steroidal calcineurin inhibitor): apply a thin layer to involved facial rash areas twice daily until resolved. Counsel that brief tingling/flushing may occur for a few seconds after application and is not an allergy. Avoid topical steroids on the face due to risk of worsening and skin thinning. 
- Continue sulfacetamide face wash; may reduce to once daily if any dryness develops (use as tolerated). 
- Continue metronidazole cream after washing. 
- Add bland moisturizer as needed (e.g., Vanicream; small amounts of petroleum jelly if very dry). 
- Medication list/coverage: Cancel pimecrolimus (Elidel) due to cost; clindamycin removed from list. Prescription for tacrolimus to Metro Market pharmacy as discussed. Refills for doxycycline and metronidazole are adequate.

2. Rosacea (facial) 
Assessment: Overlapping rosacea component with persistent mild erythema/papules; photosensitivity noted. 
Plan: 
- Continue metronidazole cream and gentle skincare; avoid anti-aging or botanical products until reassessed. 
- Reinforce sun protection (hat already in use); avoid known triggers when possible.

3. Ocular rosacea 
Assessment: History/concern for ocular involvement; preventive eyelid hygiene recommended. 
Plan: 
- Gently wash eyelids once daily with a gentle cleanser (e.g., Vanicream). 
- Use a Bruder warm compress mask as needed.

Follow-up instructions: 
- Follow up in approximately 4 weeks. 
- If rash worsens or fails to improve, call or send MyChart message sooner. 
- For a mild flare after clearance, may try tacrolimus alone for a couple of days; if insufficient, restart doxycycline per above schedule. 
- Hold off on starting any new skincare products until next visit; discuss any planned additions first.

SUBJECTIVE 
CHIEF COMPLAINT 
Left shoulder and left elbow pain. 

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS 
Mr. Jose James is a new patient presenting with constant pain in his left shoulder and left elbow for approximately five months, beginning after a fall on icy stairs in which he landed on his left side; he notes his shoulder and wrist took the brunt of the fall. Pain is worsened by lifting weights; he has been unable to lift more than 15–20 pounds and stopped gym workouts over the past 1–2 weeks due to pain. He continues to walk with his wife for about 30 minutes almost daily. He has tried icing with some relief; he has not taken any medications for pain. He denies numbness or tingling. 

"ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: 
1. Left shoulder impingement syndrome 
Assessment: Chronic left shoulder pain following a fall, with exam notable for tenderness over the left shoulder, positive Hawkins-Kennedy and Neer’s tests, abduction to 90 degrees, normal proximal/distal upper extremity strength, intact median/radial/ulnar sensation, normal empty can test, and no warmth, erythema, or deformity. Findings are consistent with subacromial impingement syndrome. 
Plan: 
- Refer to physical therapy (requested referral to Dr. Martha Rivera) at a frequency of two sessions per week, plus home exercise program as instructed by PT. 
- Continue conservative measures: rest from aggravating lifting/overhead activities and ice the shoulder. 
- If inadequate improvement after a trial of PT, consider cortisone (subacromial) injection. 
- Contact clinic if symptoms worsen or do not improve with therapy. 

2. Left elbow pain, chronic, associated with same injury 
Assessment: Left elbow tenderness on exam without warmth, erythema, deformity, or neuro deficits. Symptoms began after the same fall; may be related to overuse/biomechanical strain in the setting of shoulder pathology. 
Plan: 
- Include elbow-focused assessment/management within the prescribed physical therapy course. 
- Continue activity modification and ice as needed. 
- Monitor; patient to notify clinic if worsening or no improvement. 

Follow-up instructions: 
- PT will contact the patient within 1–2 days to schedule. 
- Patient to call or email if symptoms worsen or fail to improve with therapy.

The patient's chief complaint is pain in the left shoulder and elbow, which has been present for approximately five months since a fall while going up the stairs.

[HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS]
The patient reports that the pain started after a fall five months ago, where he fell on his left side and landed on his shoulder and wrist. Medical Reasoning: The patient's symptoms and physical examination findings are consistent with impingement syndrome of the left shoulder, which is a common condition in individuals who have experienced a fall or repetitive overhead activities.

- Follow-up: If the patient's symptoms do not improve with physical therapy, a cortisone injection may be considered.
- Patient Education: The patient is advised to continue icing the affected area, especially the shoulder, and to rest as much as possible.
- Follow-up Instructions: The patient is instructed to contact the office if symptoms worsen or do not improve with therapy.

Follow-up: The patient will be contacted by Dr. Rivera within the next day or two to schedule physical therapy sessions.

SUBJECTIVE 
CHIEF COMPLAINT 
Left shoulder and left elbow pain. 

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS 
Mr. Jose James is a new patient presenting with constant pain in his left shoulder and left elbow for approximately five months, beginning after a fall on icy stairs in which he landed on his left side; he notes his shoulder and wrist took the brunt of the fall. Pain is worsened by lifting weights; he has been unable to lift more than 15–20 pounds and stopped gym workouts over the past 1–2 weeks due to pain. He continues to walk with his wife for about 30 minutes almost daily. He has tried icing with some relief; he has not taken any medications for pain. He denies numbness or tingling. 

"ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: 
1. Left shoulder impingement syndrome 
Assessment: Chronic left shoulder pain following a fall, with exam notable for tenderness over the left shoulder, positive Hawkins-Kennedy and Neer’s tests, abduction to 90 degrees, normal proximal/distal upper extremity strength, intact median/radial/ulnar sensation, normal empty can test, and no warmth, erythema, or deformity. Findings are consistent with subacromial impingement syndrome. 
Plan: 
- Refer to physical therapy (requested referral to Dr. Martha Rivera) at a frequency of two sessions per week, plus home exercise program as instructed by PT. 
- Continue conservative measures: rest from aggravating lifting/overhead activities and ice the shoulder. 
- If inadequate improvement after a trial of PT, consider cortisone (subacromial) injection. 
- Contact clinic if symptoms worsen or do not improve with therapy. 

2. Left elbow pain, chronic, associated with same injury 
Assessment: Left elbow tenderness on exam without warmth, erythema, deformity, or neuro deficits. Symptoms began after the same fall; may be related to overuse/biomechanical strain in the setting of shoulder pathology. 
Plan: 
- Include elbow-focused assessment/management within the prescribed physical therapy course. 
- Continue activity modification and ice as needed. 
- Monitor; patient to notify clinic if worsening or no improvement. 

Follow-up instructions: 
- PT will contact the patient within 1–2 days to schedule. 
- Patient to call or email if symptoms worsen or fail to improve with therapy.

["SUBJECTIVE 
CHIEF COMPLAINT 
Upper respiratory symptoms. 
HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS 
Logan is a 57-year-old male with a history of coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG), hyperlipidemia, and OCD who presents with one week of cold symptoms that, over the last 2–3 days, have moved into his chest with congestion. He had postnasal drip at the beginning of the week which has since resolved as symptoms localized to the upper chest. He thought he might have had a slight fever but denies true fevers. He denies shortness of breath. No known sick contacts at home. He is fully vaccinated for COVID-19 (two doses). He denies chest pain other than congestion and was able to exercise prior to this illness. Diet control for cholesterol has generally been good, though less strict during recent travel. He is taking rosuvastatin (Crestor) 20 mg daily without muscle aches. 
"ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: 
1. COVID-19 infection, mild 
Assessment: Positive COVID-19 test with mild upper respiratory symptoms. Exam noted cervical lymphadenopathy and bilateral rhonchi with some wheezing; oxygenation 96%. No shortness of breath, chest pain, or persistent fever; vaccinated, suggesting a mild breakthrough infection. 
Plan: 
- Supportive management. 
- Quarantine for 10 days; avoid contact with household members as much as possible. 
- Off work during quarantine. 
- Call if symptoms worsen. 

2. Hyperlipidemia 
Assessment: Doing well on current therapy; lipid panel “really good.” No statin-associated myalgias. 
Plan: 
- Continue rosuvastatin (Crestor) 20 mg daily. 
- Continue dietary measures. 
- Order repeat lipid panel in 6 months. 

3. Coronary artery disease, s/p CABG 
Assessment: Clinically stable; exercising, no chest pain. 
Plan: 
- Continue current management. 
- Schedule a stress test in 6 months. 

Follow-up instructions: 
- Quarantine for 10 days and call if symptoms worsen. 
- Plan for lipid panel and stress test in 6 months."]

Right ankle pain after a fall while mountain biking.

- Ice the ankle for 20 minutes, five times daily. 
- Weight-bear as tolerated.
